title: Atoms into ions
html:
Guiding question

What determines the ionic nature and properties of a compound?

This topic answers three questions: how atoms become ions, why oppositely charged ions stick together, and how the giant lattice they build explains what ionic compounds are like (high melting points, brittleness, conductivity only when molten or dissolved, solubility in water).

Starter: why do atoms react at all? Think, then reveal

Most atoms do not have the electron arrangement of a noble gas: their outer (valence) level is only partly filled. By losing, gaining or sharing electrons they reach a full outer level (or full sublevels), which is a lower-energy, more stable arrangement. Losing or gaining electrons gives ions (this topic); sharing gives covalent bonds (Structure 2.2). Burning magnesium, rusting iron and sodium reacting with chlorine are all examples of atoms rearranging their outer electrons.

S2.1.1 Why atoms form ions

An atom has equal numbers of protons and electrons, so it has no overall charge. Atoms with a full outer (valence) energy level or full sublevels are especially stable, so many atoms react in a way that gives them the electron arrangement of the nearest noble gas. When an atom loses or gains electrons, the numbers of protons and electrons are no longer equal and it becomes an ion.

DefinitionAn ion is a charged particle formed when an atom (or group of atoms) loses or gains electrons. A cation is positive (electrons lost); an anion is negative (electrons gained).
Memory hook"Cat-ions are paws-itive." Metals (left of the periodic table) lose electrons and form cations; non-metals (right) gain electrons and form anions.

Sodium atom → sodium ion

Na is 2,8,1 (1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s¹, or [Ne] 3s¹). It loses its single 3s electron. The ion still has 11 protons but only 10 electrons, so its charge is 1+. Na⁺ is 1s² 2s² 2p⁶, the same as neon: the two species are isoelectronic.

Chlorine atom → chloride ion

Cl is 2,8,7 ([Ne] 3s² 3p⁵). It gains one electron to give Cl⁻, 2,8,8 (1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶), isoelectronic with argon. It now has 17 protons and 18 electrons, so its charge is 1−.

ParticleProtonsElectronsNeutronsCharge
²³Na atom1111120
²³Na⁺ ion1110121+
¹⁹F atom99100
¹⁹F⁻ ion910101−

Notice that forming an ion changes only the number of electrons. The nucleus (protons and neutrons) is unchanged.

How many electrons are there in one ⁴⁰Ca²⁺ ion?

Ca has atomic number 20, so 20 protons and (as an atom) 20 electrons. A 2+ ion has lost 2 electrons: 20 − 2 = 18 electrons. Its configuration is [2,8,8]²⁺, isoelectronic with argon. (The mass number 40 tells you the neutrons, 40 − 20 = 20, which do not change.)

How many neutrons are there in one ³⁷Cl⁻ ion?

Neutrons = mass number − atomic number = 37 − 17 = 20. Gaining an electron changes only the electron count (18), never the nucleus.

Predicting the charge of an ion

The charge of a main-group ion can be predicted from the group number, which tells you the number of valence electrons. Atoms lose or gain whichever number of electrons is smaller to reach a noble gas arrangement.

GroupValence electronsLose or gain?Ion chargeExamples
11lose 11+Li⁺, Na⁺, K⁺
22lose 22+Mg²⁺, Ca²⁺
133lose 33+Al³⁺
155gain 33−N³⁻, P³⁻
166gain 22−O²⁻, S²⁻
177gain 11−F⁻, Cl⁻, Br⁻, I⁻

Group 14 elements (C, Si) would need to lose or gain four electrons, which needs far too much energy, so they normally bond covalently instead. Group 18 elements already have full valence shells and do not form ions.

A magnesium atom has the arrangement 2,8,2. To reach a noble gas arrangement it will…

  1. gain 6 electrons
  2. lose 2 electrons
  3. gain 2 electrons
  4. lose 8 electrons

Losing 2 electrons (to [2,8]²⁺, like neon) costs far less energy than gaining 6. Metals lose electrons; gaining would give Mg⁶⁻, which never forms.

An atom has the arrangement 2,8,5. What ion does it normally form?

  1. X⁵⁺
  2. X³⁺
  3. X³⁻
  4. X⁵⁻

2,8,5 is phosphorus (group 15). Gaining 3 electrons gives 2,8,8 (like argon), so it forms P³⁻. Losing 5 would need far more energy.

Which pair of species is isoelectronic?

  1. Na⁺ and Ne
  2. Na and Ne
  3. Cl⁻ and Ne
  4. K⁺ and Ne

Na⁺ has 10 electrons (2,8), the same as Ne. Cl⁻ and K⁺ both have 18 electrons, so they are isoelectronic with Ar, not Ne.

Transition element ions and ionic radius

Transition elements often form more than one ion (variable oxidation states), e.g. Fe²⁺ and Fe³⁺, Cu⁺ and Cu²⁺. The charge is shown with a Roman numeral in the name: iron(III) oxide is Fe₂O₃. Other common ions worth knowing: Zn²⁺, Ag⁺, Pb²⁺ (and Pb⁴⁺).

Key pointTransition metal atoms lose their 4s electrons before their 3d electrons, even though 4s fills first. Fe is [Ar] 4s² 3d⁶, so Fe²⁺ is [Ar] 3d⁶ and Fe³⁺ is [Ar] 3d⁵.
Predict first: write the configuration of Cu²⁺, then reveal

Cu is [Ar] 4s¹ 3d¹⁰. Remove the 4s electron first, then one 3d electron: Cu²⁺ is [Ar] 3d⁹. A common wrong answer is [Ar] 4s² 3d⁷, which removes 3d electrons before 4s.

Linking note (AHL, Structure 1.3)The successive ionization energies of transition elements rise gradually across the 4s and 3d electrons because they are close in energy. Several of them can be removed for a similar energy cost, which is why transition elements show variable oxidation states.

Ionic radius. A cation is smaller than its parent atom (it has lost its outer shell and the remaining electrons are pulled in more tightly by the same nuclear charge). An anion is larger than its parent atom (extra electron–electron repulsion with the same nuclear charge). Ionic radii are listed in the data booklet; they matter for lattice enthalpy (lesson 4).

Which list is in order of increasing radius?

  1. Na⁺ < Na < Cl < Cl⁻
  2. Na < Na⁺ < Cl⁻ < Cl
  3. Cl⁻ < Cl < Na⁺ < Na
  4. Na⁺ < Cl⁻ < Na < Cl

Na⁺ has lost its whole third shell, so it is smallest. Na is larger than Cl (same period, Na has 6 fewer protons pulling the outer shell). Cl⁻ is larger than Cl because the extra electron increases repulsion with the same 17 protons.

title: The ionic bond and dot-and-cross diagrams
html:
S2.1.2 The ionic bond

When a metal reacts with a non-metal, electrons are transferred from the metal atoms to the non-metal atoms. The ions formed have opposite charges and attract each other. For sodium and chlorine, each sodium atom loses one electron and each chlorine atom gains one; both end up as stable ions with noble gas arrangements.

DefinitionAn ionic bond is the electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions (cations and anions).
Common mistakeThe transfer of electrons is how the ions are formed; it is not the bond. The bond is the attraction between the ions. In a 2-mark "describe ionic bonding" question you usually need both: (1) electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions; (2) the ions form by transfer of electrons from metal to non-metal. Mark schemes do not accept "attraction between metals and non-metals": say ions.

Which statement best describes ionic bonding?

  1. Electrostatic attraction between positive ions and delocalized electrons, formed by electron transfer
  2. Electrostatic attraction between positive ions and negative ions, formed by electron transfer
  3. Electrostatic attraction between positive ions and negative ions, formed by electron sharing
  4. Electrostatic attraction between nuclei and a shared pair of electrons

Ions of opposite charge attract; the ions come from electron transfer. Option A describes metallic bonding and option D covalent bonding.

Ionic bonding is most likely when the metal has a low ionization energy (loses electrons easily) and the non-metal has a high electronegativity (attracts electrons strongly). The bigger the electronegativity difference (ΔEN) between the two elements, the more ionic the bond. As a rough guide, a ΔEN above about 1.8 gives mainly ionic character. In reality there is a continuum between ionic and covalent bonding; this is developed with the bonding triangle in Structure 2.4.

Careful with "always"You will often hear "ionic bonding is between a metal and a non-metal". That is a useful first test, but not a rule without exceptions: ammonium salts such as NH₄Cl and NH₄NO₃ are ionic although they contain no metal, because NH₄⁺ is a cation.
Linking note (Reactivity 3.2)Forming an ionic compound from its elements is a redox reaction: the metal is oxidized (loses electrons) and the non-metal is reduced (gains electrons). E.g. 2Na(s) + Cl₂(g) → 2NaCl(s); 2K(s) + Cl₂(g) → 2KCl(s).

Drawing ionic bonding (Lewis / dot-and-cross diagrams)

Show the outer shell of each atom, use an arrow to show which electrons move, then draw the ions in square brackets with the charge at the top right. After transfer, the metal ion is usually drawn with an empty (or no) outer shell and the non-metal ion with a full octet of dots and crosses. Use dots for one atom's electrons and crosses for the other's so the examiner can see where each electron came from.

Work through four questions for every compound: What group is each element in? How many outer electrons? Lose or gain, and how many? So what charge? Then balance the charges.

Worked example · Magnesium chlorideShow how magnesium and chlorine form magnesium chloride.
Mg is group 2: 2 valence electrons → loses 2 → Mg²⁺
Cl is group 17: 7 valence electrons → gains 1 → Cl⁻
One Mg atom gives one electron to each of two Cl atoms
Diagram: [Mg]²⁺ 2 × [Cl (8 electrons: 7 dots + 1 cross)]⁻
Formula: MgCl₂

Practise with: MgO, LiCl, Na₂O, MgF₂, AlCl₃, Al₂O₃, Mg₃N₂, Al₂S₃, CaCl₂. Draw each yourself, then check against the diagrams below.

Exam-style: describe what happens when potassium reacts with fluorine to form KF [5]
  • A potassium atom loses one electron (its 4s electron)…
  • …forming a positive ion, K⁺;
  • a fluorine atom gains one electron…
  • …forming a negative ion, F⁻;
  • the oppositely charged ions attract (electrostatic attraction = ionic bond).

Mark schemes cap you if you call the particles the wrong thing (for example "fluoride atom" or "potassium molecule"), so name atoms and ions precisely.

Exam-style: describe how a calcium atom and an oxygen atom form calcium oxide, giving the charges [4]

Calcium loses electrons and oxygen gains electrons; two electrons are transferred; the calcium ion has a 2+ charge; the oxide ion has a 2− charge.

title: Formulae, names and polyatomic ions
html:
Deducing formulae of ionic compounds

An ionic compound is electrically neutral overall, so the total positive charge must equal the total negative charge.

  1. Write the two ions with their charges.
  2. Find the lowest number of each that makes the total charge zero (the "swap and drop" shortcut: the charge number of one ion becomes the subscript of the other, then simplify).
  3. Put brackets around a polyatomic ion if more than one is needed.
Worked example · FormulaeLithium oxide: Li⁺ and O²⁻ → need 2 Li⁺ → Li₂O
Calcium nitride: Ca²⁺ and N³⁻ → 3 × (2+) = 6+, 2 × (3−) = 6− → Ca₃N₂
Aluminium oxide: Al³⁺ and O²⁻ → 2 × (3+) = 6+, 3 × (2−) = 6− → Al₂O₃
Ammonium sulfate: NH₄⁺ and SO₄²⁻ → (NH₄)₂SO₄
Calcium phosphate: Ca²⁺ and PO₄³⁻ → Ca₃(PO₄)₂

What is the formula of the ionic compound formed when calcium and nitrogen react?

  1. Ca₂N₃
  2. Ca₃N₂
  3. Ca₅N₂
  4. Ca₂N₅

Ca²⁺ and N³⁻: the lowest common multiple of 2 and 3 is 6, so 3 Ca²⁺ (6+) balance 2 N³⁻ (6−): Ca₃N₂. Ca₂N₃ is the classic swap error.

Exam tipIf you are told the formula of one compound of a metal, you can deduce its charge and use it. E.g. cerium(III) sulfate is Ce₂(SO₄)₃, so Ce is 3+ and cerium(III) phosphate is CePO₄ (3+ and 3− in a 1:1 ratio). A metal M that forms MCO₃ is M²⁺, so its sulfate is MSO₄.

Naming ionic compounds

  • Binary ionic compounds (two elements): name the metal cation first, then the non-metal anion with the ending -ide. MgO magnesium oxide; NaCl sodium chloride; Li₃N lithium nitride; ZnS zinc sulfide.
  • Compounds with a polyatomic anion containing oxygen usually end in -ate (or -ite for fewer oxygens): Mg(NO₃)₂ magnesium nitrate; CuSO₄ copper(II) sulfate; NiSO₄ nickel(II) sulfate; Al(BrO₃)₃ aluminium bromate.
  • Give the oxidation state in Roman numerals for metals with variable charge: FeCl₂ iron(II) chloride, FeCl₃ iron(III) chloride; SnO tin(II) oxide but SnO₂ tin(IV) oxide; NiI₂ nickel(II) iodide.

IB uses the spellings sulfide, sulfate, sulfur (not "sulph-").

Polyatomic ions to learn

A polyatomic ion is a group of covalently bonded atoms carrying an overall charge. The bonding within the ion is covalent; the bonding between the ion and its counter-ion is ionic. So compounds like NaOH, CaCO₃ and NH₄NO₃ contain both ionic and covalent bonds.

IonFormulaIonFormula
ammoniumNH₄⁺hydroxideOH⁻
nitrateNO₃⁻hydrogencarbonateHCO₃⁻
carbonateCO₃²⁻sulfateSO₄²⁻
phosphatePO₄³⁻ethanoateCH₃COO⁻
dichromate(VI)Cr₂O₇²⁻chromate(VI)CrO₄²⁻
manganate(VII)MnO₄⁻sulfiteSO₃²⁻
Exam tipIf you forget a charge, work it out from oxidation states: carbonate, C = +4 and 3 × O = −6, so CO₃ is 2−; sulfate, S = +6 and 4 × O = −8, so SO₄ is 2−; nitrate, N = +5 and 3 × O = −6, so NO₃ is 1−. Make flashcards and test a friend.
Common mistakeSulfate (SO₄²⁻) is an anion, not a cation. Ammonium, NH₄⁺, is the only common polyatomic cation. Hydrogencarbonate is HCO₃⁻ (1−), not 2−. Ethanoate is CH₃COO⁻.

Which set of formulas for nitrate, phosphate, carbonate and ammonium is correct?

  1. NO₃⁻, PO₄³⁻, CO₃⁻, NH₄⁺
  2. NO₃²⁻, PO₃²⁻, CO₃²⁻, NH₃⁺
  3. NO₃⁻, PO₄³⁻, CO₃²⁻, NH₄⁺
  4. NO₃²⁻, PO₃³⁻, CO₃⁻, NH₄⁺

Nitrate NO₃⁻, phosphate PO₄³⁻, carbonate CO₃²⁻, ammonium NH₄⁺. Check with oxidation states: P = +5, 4 O = −8, so PO₄ is 3−.

Which compounds contain both ionic and covalent bonding? I. CaCO₃ II. NaCl III. NaOH

  1. I and II only
  2. I and III only
  3. II and III only
  4. I, II and III

CaCO₃ and NaOH contain polyatomic ions (CO₃²⁻, OH⁻) held together by covalent bonds, plus ionic bonds between the ions. NaCl has only ionic bonding.

Fill the gaps: Calcium nitrate contains Ca²⁺ ions and NO₃⁻ ions. The force between these ions is electrostatic attraction, while the bonds inside the nitrate ion are covalent.

Challenge: write the formulae of tin(IV) oxide, aluminium sulfide, ammonium phosphate and iron(III) hydroxide

SnO₂ (Sn⁴⁺, O²⁻); Al₂S₃ (2 × 3+ = 6+, 3 × 2− = 6−); (NH₄)₃PO₄ (3 × 1+ balances 3−); Fe(OH)₃ (brackets because more than one OH⁻).

title: Ionic lattices and lattice enthalpy
html:
S2.1.3 Ionic lattices

An ionic bond is a strong electrostatic attraction, and it acts equally in all directions, so ions do not pair up as isolated molecules. Instead, each ion attracts as many oppositely charged ions as can pack around it, and the arrangement repeats in three dimensions until the ions run out. This giant 3D structure is an ionic lattice.

  • In sodium chloride each Na⁺ is surrounded by six Cl⁻ ions arranged octahedrally, and each Cl⁻ by six Na⁺ ions. The lattice is cubic, which is why salt crystals are cubes.
  • Because there are no discrete molecules, ionic compounds are represented by empirical formulae (formula units) showing the simplest ratio of ions, e.g. NaCl, MgCl₂. Do not call them "molecules".
  • The lattice is neutral overall because the total positive and negative charges are equal, even though it contains huge numbers of ions.

How many Cl⁻ ions surround each Na⁺ ion in a sodium chloride lattice?

  1. 2
  2. 4
  3. 6
  4. 8

Six, arranged octahedrally (above, below, left, right, front, back). Each Cl⁻ is likewise surrounded by six Na⁺. This is called 6:6 coordination.

Exam-style: what is meant by the term ionic lattice? [2]

A regular / repeating (3D) arrangement…

…of oppositely charged ions (positive and negative ions, cations and anions).

Which substances have an ionic lattice in the solid state? I. silicon dioxide II. sodium fluoride III. ammonium nitrate

  1. I and II only
  2. I and III only
  3. II and III only
  4. I, II and III

NaF (metal + non-metal) and NH₄NO₃ (ammonium cation + nitrate anion) are ionic. SiO₂ is a giant covalent network (Structure 2.2), not ionic.

Lattice enthalpy

DefinitionThe lattice enthalpy (ΔHlat) is the standard enthalpy change when one mole of an ionic compound is separated into its gaseous ions. It is always endothermic (positive), e.g. NaCl(s) → Na⁺(g) + Cl⁻(g), ΔHlat = +790 kJ mol⁻¹.

Lattice enthalpy measures the strength of ionic bonding: the larger the value, the stronger the attraction between the ions. It depends on two factors:

  1. Ionic charge: higher charges attract more strongly, so lattice enthalpy increases sharply with charge.
  2. Ionic radius: smaller ions can get closer together, so their centres of charge are nearer and the attraction is stronger.
Lattice enthalpy ∝ (charge of cation × charge of anion) / (sum of ionic radii)
CompoundIonsΔHlat / kJ mol⁻¹ (approx.)Reason
NaFNa⁺, F⁻930F⁻ is the smallest halide ion
NaClNa⁺, Cl⁻790Cl⁻ larger than F⁻
NaINa⁺, I⁻705I⁻ largest, weakest attraction
KClK⁺, Cl⁻720K⁺ larger than Na⁺
MgOMg²⁺, O²⁻3791both ions doubly charged and small
Worked example · Ranking lattice enthalpiesExplain why MgO has a much higher lattice enthalpy than NaCl.
Charges: Mg²⁺/O²⁻ (product 4) vs Na⁺/Cl⁻ (product 1)
Radii: Mg²⁺ smaller than Na⁺; O²⁻ smaller than Cl⁻
Higher charges and smaller ions → stronger electrostatic attraction
→ much more energy needed to separate the ions → larger ΔHlat

Using the table, how many times larger is the lattice enthalpy of MgO than that of NaCl? (Give your answer to 2 significant figures.)

3791 ÷ 790 = 4.8. The charge product alone (2 × 2 = 4 compared with 1 × 1 = 1) predicts about 4 times; the smaller radii of Mg²⁺ and O²⁻ push it higher still.

Which compound has the largest lattice enthalpy?

  1. KBr
  2. NaCl
  3. CaO
  4. CaCl₂

CaO has two doubly charged ions (product 4) and O²⁻ is small. CaCl₂ has Ca²⁺ but singly charged, larger Cl⁻ ions; KBr and NaCl have charge product 1.

Which ordering of lattice enthalpy is correct?

  1. NaI > NaCl > NaF
  2. NaF > NaCl > NaI
  3. NaCl > NaF > NaI
  4. all three are equal, because the charges are equal

The charges are the same, so radius decides. F⁻ < Cl⁻ < I⁻ in size, so attraction (and lattice enthalpy) falls from NaF to NaI.

Linking noteLattice enthalpies cannot be measured directly; they are found from Born–Haber cycles (Reactivity 1.2, AHL). Values are in the data booklet. Lattice enthalpy and the bonding continuum also explain the trend in melting points of the period 3 chlorides (Structure 3.1).

title: Properties of ionic compounds
html:
Physical properties of ionic compounds

Every property of an ionic compound can be explained from two facts: the lattice is held together by many strong electrostatic attractions acting in all directions, and the ions are fixed in place in the solid but free to move when molten or dissolved.

PropertyObservationExplanation in terms of structure
Volatility (melting / boiling point)Low volatility: high m.p. and b.p. (NaCl melts at about 800 °C)Many strong electrostatic attractions act in all directions throughout the giant lattice; a lot of energy is needed to overcome them. Higher lattice enthalpy → higher melting point.
Electrical conductivityDo not conduct as solids; conduct when molten or in aqueous solutionIn the solid the ions are fixed in place. When molten or dissolved, the ions are free to move and carry charge. (Ions, not electrons, carry the current.)
SolubilityOften soluble in water (polar solvent); insoluble in non-polar solvents such as hexanePolar water molecules are attracted to the ions (δ− O towards cations, δ+ H towards anions). These ion–dipole attractions release energy that helps pull ions out of the lattice. Non-polar solvents cannot interact with ions in this way.
BrittlenessHard but shatter when hitA force shifts one layer of ions relative to the next so that ions of the same charge line up; the like charges repel and the crystal splits.

Melting and boiling points

Key point"Low volatility" means a high boiling point: volatility is the tendency to evaporate. A lower boiling point means a higher volatility. Ionic compounds have low volatility.

Brittleness

Electrical conductivity

To conduct, a substance needs mobile charged particles (ions or delocalized electrons). An ionic solid has charged particles but they cannot move.

Reveal the answers to the four particle diagrams
  1. Ionic solid: does not conduct; ions are fixed in the lattice.
  2. Pure water: essentially does not conduct; it is made of neutral molecules (only a tiny number of ions from self-ionization).
  3. Dissolved ionic solid: conducts; the ions are separated by water molecules and are free to move.
  4. Molten ionic solid: conducts; the ions are free to move.
Common mistakeSaying solid ionic compounds do not conduct "because they have no free electrons" loses the mark. The correct reason is that the ions cannot move in the solid. Also, ionic compounds do not have "intermolecular forces": there are no molecules.

Comparing sodium and sodium chloride. Both conduct electricity, but differently. In sodium metal (solid or liquid), delocalized electrons move and no chemical change happens. In molten sodium chloride, ions move to the electrodes and are discharged, so a chemical change (electrolysis) occurs: Na⁺ + e⁻ → Na at the cathode and 2Cl⁻ → Cl₂ + 2e⁻ at the anode.

Sodium (metal)Sodium chloride (molten)
Particles carrying the currentdelocalized electronsions (Na⁺ and Cl⁻)
Conducts as a solid?yesno
Chemical change at electrodes?noyes (Na and Cl₂ produced)

Solubility

Water molecules are polar: overall neutral, but with a partial negative charge on O and partial positive charges on H. The δ− oxygen ends are attracted to cations and the δ+ hydrogen ends to anions, so water molecules can surround ions and pull them away from the lattice. Once dissolved, the ions are free to move, so the solution conducts. (This is why water is said to "attract the ions away from the lattice"; it is not that water carries a charge.)

Why does solid sodium chloride not conduct electricity?

  1. It has no free electrons
  2. Its ions are not free to move
  3. It has no charged particles
  4. Its intermolecular forces are too strong

The charged particles (ions) are present but locked in the lattice. "No free electrons" is not credited; there are no intermolecular forces in an ionic compound.

Which property is NOT typical of an ionic compound such as MgCl₂?

  1. High melting point
  2. Soluble in water
  3. Conducts electricity when solid
  4. Conducts electricity in aqueous solution

Ionic solids do not conduct: ions are fixed. They conduct only when molten or dissolved.

True or false: ionic compounds have low melting points and do not conduct when molten.

  1. True
  2. False

False on both counts: ionic compounds have high melting points and conduct when molten because the ions can move.

Practical: investigating the properties of sodium chloride

A simple class practical tests the properties above:

  • Look at salt grains under a hand lens or microscope: they are cubic with similar angles, showing a regular arrangement of particles.
  • Heat crystals strongly in a boiling tube: they do not melt in a Bunsen flame, showing strong bonding (high melting point).
  • Stir into water: it dissolves.
  • Test conductivity with carbon electrodes and a bulb: the solid does not conduct; the solution does, showing the particles are charged ions that become mobile.
Data question: calcium iodide has a very high boiling point, does not conduct as a solid and conducts when molten. Phosphorus has a low boiling point and does not conduct in any state and is insoluble. Which is ionic, and what evidence shows it?

Calcium iodide is ionic: it conducts when molten but not when solid (ions become mobile only on melting), and it has a very high boiling point (strong electrostatic attractions in a giant lattice). Calcium iodide is also soluble in water. Phosphorus is simple molecular: low boiling point because only weak intermolecular forces are overcome, and no ions or delocalized electrons, so it never conducts.

Typical exam questions and how to answer them

  • "Describe the ionic bonding in KCl and how the ions are formed." [2] Electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions (K⁺ and Cl⁻); formed by transfer of an electron from a K atom to a Cl atom.
  • "Explain why sodium oxide has a higher melting point than sulfur trioxide." [3] Na₂O is a giant ionic lattice with strong electrostatic attractions between ions; SO₃ is simple molecular with weak intermolecular forces; much more energy is needed to break the ionic lattice.
  • "Explain the electrical conductivity of molten sodium oxide and liquid sulfur trioxide." [2] Molten Na₂O conducts because its ions are mobile; liquid SO₃ does not because it consists of neutral molecules with no mobile charged particles.
  • "Which compounds have an ionic lattice?" Look for a metal or the ammonium ion. NaF and NH₄NO₃ are ionic; SiO₂ is giant covalent.
  • Formula questions. Lithium and selenium → Li₂Se; aluminium and oxygen → Al₂O₃; magnesium fluoride → MgF₂.
  • "Explain, in terms of bonding, why KBrF₄ has a high melting point." [3] It is ionic: strong electrostatic attractions between oppositely charged ions (K⁺ and BrF₄⁻), so a lot of energy is needed to overcome them. Saying "strong covalent bonds" scores nothing, because the covalent bonds inside BrF₄⁻ are not broken on melting.

Summary checklist

  • Predict ion charges from the group number; write configurations of ions (4s before 3d for transition metals).
  • Define an ionic bond as electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions.
  • Deduce formulae and names, including polyatomic ions and Roman numerals.
  • Describe the 3D lattice and why empirical formulae are used.
  • Define lattice enthalpy (endothermic, gaseous ions) and explain the effect of charge and radius.
  • Explain volatility, conductivity, solubility and brittleness from the lattice structure.
